step1_summary: Chief complaint: Burning/stinging pain with urination, increased urinary frequency, and lower abdominal (suprapubic) ache for just under 1 week.

Symptoms: Dysuria and frequency started ≈6–7 days ago; today noted pink-tinged urine (possible hematuria). Pain is described as aching, worse while voiding, localized to lower abdomen; does not radiate to back/flank. No nausea, vomiting, fever, chills, or flank pain reported. No abnormal vaginal discharge. Bowel habit unchanged from baseline IBS.
Past medical history: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). No known kidney/bladder problems.
Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill; Mebeverine (antispasmodic for IBS).
Family history: Negative for renal or bladder disease (other significant FHx not mentioned).

Social history: 19-year-old female university student living in halls. Long-term boyfriend; sexually active with unprotected intercourse ~1 week ago. Social alcohol use; tried cannabis once 1.5 weeks ago. Non-smoker otherwise.
Vital signs / physical exam: None taken (telephone consult). Patient denies subjective fever.
Labs / imaging: None yet; plan to submit mid-stream urine for dipstick/culture.

V: Ureteric or bladder calculus with microtrauma → hematuria & dysuria (frequency and pain possible if stone near bladder neck).
Renal papillary necrosis (rare in this age) causing hematuria—but no risk factors stated.
I: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (bacterial UTI)—classic dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, microhematuria.
Urethritis / cervicitis from Chlamydia or Gonorrhoea—dysuria ± hematuria, sexual activity risk.
Acute pyelonephritis—infection ascending to kidney; would add fever/flank pain (less likely here).
N: Bladder or urethral tumour—can cause hematuria/dysuria, but exceedingly rare at 19 y.
D: Early interstitial cystitis (painful bladder syndrome)—frequency, suprapubic pain, sterile urine.
Vitamin C deficiency causing fragile vessels/hematuria (very unlikely).
I2: Drug-induced cystitis/hematuria (e.g., cyclophosphamide)—no offending meds reported.
Chemical irritation from new substance (e.g., cannabis contaminants)—implausible.
C: Congenital urinary tract anomaly pre-disposing to infection (e.g., vesicoureteral reflux)—no history but possible.
A: Autoimmune cystitis (e.g., lupus cystitis)—rare, no systemic features.
T: Mechanical trauma to urethra/bladder (recent intercourse)—can cause transient hematuria/dysuria.
E: Diabetic glycosuria causing frequency, but dysuria & hematuria unexplained; no diabetes history.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of dysuria, urinary frequency, and suprapubic discomfort for <1 week in a young woman, with mild hematuria and no systemic signs suggests lower urinary tract infection.
supporting_evidence: Suprapubic aching pain, worse while voiding
No fever or flank pain → localizes infection to bladder
opposing_evidence: No urine culture yet—possible sterile pyuria or alternative cause

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Sexually active woman with unprotected intercourse and dysuria ± minimal hematuria; STIs can mimic cystitis and may lack vaginal discharge.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal discomfort possible with cervicitis/PID
opposing_evidence: No vaginal discharge, spotting, or pelvic pain beyond voiding
No mention of dyspareunia, intermenstrual bleeding

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Stone near bladder can cause dysuria, frequency, and hematuria; pain may be mild suprapubic when stone is intravesical.
supporting_evidence: Urinary frequency and dysuria possible if stone irritates bladder neck
opposing_evidence: No colicky flank/loin pain or radiation typical of stones
Symptoms started gradually and are mild; stones usually produce severe colic
Age 19 without metabolic risk factors—stones less common

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Chronic sterile bladder pain with frequency and dysuria; possible in young females but usually longstanding, not acute onset.
Ascending infection would account for dysuria & hematuria, but lacking systemic or flank signs.
supporting_evidence: Lower UTI symptoms could progress upward
opposing_evidence: No fever, chills, nausea/vomiting, or costovertebral angle pain
